passage:
A plant cannot walk away from the spot where it grows, yet its seeds often end up far from home. Why does this matter? If every seed fell straight down, the young plants would crowd around their parent. They would have to compete for sunlight, water, and space in the soil. So plants have found clever ways to send their seeds on long trips.

Some seeds ride the wind. A dandelion seed hangs from a tiny tuft of soft threads that works like a parachute, so a light breeze can carry it across a whole field. Maple seeds have a flat wing on one side. When they drop, they spin like little helicopters and drift away from the tree.

Other seeds travel by water. A coconut has a thick, hollow husk that lets it float. It can bob on the ocean for weeks before it washes up on a faraway beach, where it may sprout into a new palm tree.

Animals are helpful travel partners, too. Burdock seeds are covered in tiny hooks that catch on a passing dog's fur or a hiker's socks. The seeds get carried a long way before they finally fall off. Birds eat berries and later drop the seeds in new places.

Some plants do not wait for help at all. When the pods of certain plants dry out, they suddenly twist and burst open, and the seeds shoot out like popcorn jumping from a hot pan.

Wind, water, animals, or a sudden pop: each of these methods helps a seed find room to grow.

passage:
Have you ever noticed that the Moon seems to change shape from night to night? One week it looks like a thin silver smile, and a week or so later it is a bright, round circle. But the Moon itself never changes shape at all; it is always a ball of rock. What changes is how much of its sunny side we are able to see.

The Moon does not make its own light. Like a mirror, it reflects light that comes from the Sun. At every moment, half of the Moon is lit by sunlight, while the other half remains dark. As the Moon travels around Earth, we see different amounts of the lit half. These different views are called phases.

When the Moon is between Earth and the Sun, its bright side faces away from us, so we see almost nothing. This is called a new moon. Over the next two weeks, a little more of the lit side comes into view each night. First we see a thin sliver called a crescent, then we see half of the Moon's face, and later we see almost all of it. At last, when Earth is between the Sun and the Moon, we see the whole bright side. This is called a full moon.

After the full moon, the pattern runs backward. The lit part shrinks night by night until the new moon comes back, and the whole cycle takes about twenty-nine and a half days.

Long ago, people used this steady, repeating pattern to keep track of time. In fact, the English word "month" comes from an old word for "moon." So the next time you look up at night, remember that you are looking at a calendar in the sky.

passage:
Today, almost every pencil has a pink eraser on its end. But for a long time, people who made mistakes with pencils had a messy problem. To remove a pencil mark, they rubbed it with a ball of damp bread. The bread picked up the gray marks, but it also left crumbs everywhere. Worse, the bread could grow moldy if it sat too long.

In the 1700s, explorers brought a strange material to Europe from South America. It came from the sticky sap of certain trees. A popular story says that in 1770, an English engineer reached for his bread to fix a mistake. By accident, he grabbed a piece of this tree material instead. To his surprise, it erased the mark very well! Around the same time, a scientist noticed the same thing. Because the material could rub out pencil marks, he called it "rubber." That is how rubber got its name.

Early rubber erasers had problems, though. In hot weather they turned soft and gooey. In cold weather they became hard and cracked. Then, in the 1840s, inventors learned to heat rubber with a yellow mineral called sulfur. This made the rubber strong and bendy in any weather.

Finally, in 1858, an American inventor had a simple idea. He attached an eraser right onto the end of a pencil. Now a writer never had to hunt for an eraser again.

The next time you fix a mistake, think of all the steps it took to make that little eraser.

passage:
Every fall, gray squirrels get very busy. They gather acorns and other nuts and bury them in the ground. A single squirrel may hide thousands of nuts in one season. Instead of keeping them all in one pile, it digs a separate small hole for almost every nut. Scientists call this scatter hoarding.

Why spread the nuts out? If a squirrel kept all its food in one place, a hungry thief could steal everything at once. With nuts hidden in many spots, a thief can find only a few.

Scientists have watched squirrels closely to learn how they find their nuts again in winter. Squirrels have a strong sense of smell, which helps them sniff out buried food. But smell is not the whole story. Studies show that squirrels also remember where they dug. They seem to use trees, rocks, and other landmarks like a map.

Squirrels can also be sneaky. In some studies, scientists saw that when a squirrel knew another animal was watching, it would dig a hole and pretend to drop in a nut. Then it would cover the empty hole and carry the real nut somewhere else. The watcher would be tricked into searching an empty spot.

Even the smartest squirrel does not find every nut. Some stay buried all winter. In spring, these forgotten nuts may sprout into new trees. In this way, busy squirrels help plant the forests they live in.

Why spread the nuts out? If a squirrel kept all its food in one place, a hungry thief could steal everything at once. With nuts hidden in many spots, a thief can find only a few.

Scientists have watched squirrels closely to learn how they find their nuts again in winter. Squirrels have a strong sense of smell, which helps them sniff out buried food. But smell is not the whole story. Studies show that squirrels also remember where they dug. They seem to use trees, rocks, and other landmarks like a map.

Squirrels can also be sneaky. In some studies, scientists saw that when a squirrel knew another animal was watching, it would dig a hole and pretend to drop in a nut. Then it would cover the empty hole and carry the real nut somewhere else. The watcher would be tricked into searching an empty spot.

Even the smartest squirrel does not find every nut. Some stay buried all winter. In spring, these forgotten nuts may sprout into new trees. In this way, busy squirrels help plant the forests they live in.
stem: According to the passage, what may happen to nuts that squirrels never find?
choices: They may be found by birds.
They may wash away in the rain.
They may grow into new trees.
They may turn into stones.
explanation: The last paragraph says, "In spring, these forgotten nuts may sprout into new trees."

Mina pressed her hands around the lump of wet clay and pushed the pedal with her foot, and the potter's wheel began to hum and spin. "Gently," said Grandpa Joon from the stool beside her. "Let the clay find its center."

Mina did not feel gentle at all. She had watched Grandpa make bowls all summer, and he made it look as easy as stirring soup. She wanted her own bowl to be finished before her parents arrived to pick her up, so she pressed harder. The clay wobbled for a moment, then flopped over sideways like a tired puppy.

"Ugh, it's ruined!" Mina groaned.

Grandpa did not laugh; instead, he scooped up the clay, patted it into a smooth ball, and set it back in the middle of the wheel. "Do you know how many bowls I ruined when I was learning?" he asked. "More than there are stars over the lake."

Mina looked at him in surprise, because she had always imagined that Grandpa was simply born knowing how to do this.

She tried again, and this time she kept her elbows steady against her knees and let the spinning wheel do most of the work. She thought about the clay instead of the clock, and slowly the lump rose into a short, thick cup, although one side was a little lower than the other.

"It's crooked," she said with a sigh.

"It's yours," Grandpa answered with a smile. "And tomorrow it will be a little less crooked."

When her parents finally arrived, Mina was still sitting at the wheel, her hands gray with clay, and for once she did not ask to go home early.
stem: Which of the following best states a lesson of the story?
choices: It is best to finish every job as fast as possible.
Only people who are born with talent can make art.
A crooked cup is not worth keeping.
Learning a new skill takes patience and practice.
explanation: Mina fails when she rushes, succeeds when she slows down, and learns that Grandpa "ruined" many bowls while learning.

passage:
In the early 1800s, the cliffs near the small English seaside town of Lyme Regis were crumbling. Storms and waves regularly tore away chunks of rock, and with them came strange shapes: coiled shells, bony spines, and teeth set in stone. Most visitors saw curiosities. Mary Anning saw a living.

Anning was born in 1799 into a poor family. Her father, a cabinetmaker, collected fossils on the beach and sold them to tourists, and he taught his children to do the same. When he died in 1810, the family was left deep in debt, and selling fossils became a matter of survival rather than a hobby. The work was risky. The best finds appeared after storms, exactly when landslides were most likely, and Anning herself once barely escaped a falling section of cliff.

Her first major discovery came when she was about twelve. After her brother found an unusual skull, Mary spent months carefully digging out the rest of the skeleton. It belonged to a creature that looked partly like a fish and partly like a lizard. Scientists later named it Ichthyosaurus, meaning "fish lizard." In 1823 she uncovered the first nearly complete skeleton of a plesiosaur, a sea reptile with a tiny head, a very long neck, and four paddle-like flippers. The find was so odd that one famous expert at first suspected it was a fake. After careful study, he admitted that he had been wrong.

Anning was more than a skilled digger. She taught herself anatomy, cut open modern fish to compare them with fossils, and noticed details that others missed. She recognized, for example, that certain stones found inside skeletons were actually fossilized droppings, which revealed what ancient animals had eaten.

Despite these achievements, Anning was largely shut out of the scientific world. Women were not allowed to join the leading geological society of her day, and the wealthy men who bought her specimens often published descriptions of them without mentioning her name. She struggled with money for much of her life.

Recognition came slowly. Near the end of her life, members of the geological society collected money to support her, and after her death in 1847, its president honored her in a public speech. Today, historians count her among the founders of paleontology, the study of ancient life. Her story is proof that important science can begin on a windswept beach with a hammer and a sharp eye.

explanation: The passage describes her discoveries and skills while stressing that she was poor, "shut out of the scientific world," and recognized only slowly.

Around the year 1700, an instrument maker named Bartolomeo Cristofori was working in Florence, Italy, for a wealthy family that loved music. The most popular keyboard instrument of the day was the harpsichord. When a player pressed one of its keys, a small quill inside plucked a metal string. The harpsichord made a bright, sparkling sound, but it had one major limitation: no matter how hard or how softly a musician pressed the keys, the notes came out at nearly the same volume.

Cristofori set out to solve this problem. Instead of plucking the strings, his new instrument struck them with small hammers covered in leather. A gentle touch on a key sent the hammer moving slowly, producing a quiet note; a firm touch sent it flying, producing a loud one. For the first time, a keyboard player could make the music swell and fade simply by changing the pressure of the fingers.

Building such an instrument was far trickier than it sounds. If a hammer stayed pressed against a string, it would stop the vibration and kill the sound at once. Cristofori designed a clever device, now called an escapement, that let each hammer strike its string and then instantly fall back, allowing the note to ring. He also added dampers, small pads that settled onto the strings to silence them when the player let go of a key.

Cristofori called his invention a "harpsichord with soft and loud." In Italian, the words for soft and loud are piano and forte, so the instrument became known as the pianoforte, a name later shortened to piano.

Surprisingly, the invention did not catch on right away. Early pianos were fairly quiet, and many musicians preferred the familiar harpsichord. Over the next century, however, builders in Germany, Austria, and England improved the design. They made the frames sturdier, the strings thicker, and the hammers heavier, and they eventually covered the hammers with felt for a warmer tone. Composers began writing music that took advantage of the piano's range, with sudden contrasts between whispering and thundering passages.

By the 1800s, the piano had pushed the harpsichord aside and become the centerpiece of concert halls and family parlors alike. Every time a pianist plays a note softly, he or she is using the idea Cristofori had more than three hundred years ago.

explanation: The first paragraph says that however hard or softly the keys were pressed, "the notes came out at nearly the same volume," and the second says Cristofori "set out to solve this problem."

passage:
A glacier may look like a frozen, motionless mountain of ice, but it is actually a slow-moving river. Understanding how glaciers form and travel helps explain the shapes of many landscapes around the world, including places where no ice remains today.

Glaciers begin with snow. In very cold regions, such as high mountains or lands near the poles, more snow falls in winter than melts in summer. Year after year, new layers pile up. The weight of the upper layers presses down on the older snow beneath, squeezing out the air between the flakes. Gradually, the fluffy snow turns into grainy, packed material and finally into dense, bluish ice. This process can take many decades.

Once the ice becomes thick enough, it begins to move under its own weight. Gravity pulls it downhill, and the enormous pressure at the bottom allows the ice to bend and flow slowly, almost like extremely thick honey. Most glaciers creep only a few centimeters to a few meters a day, though some occasionally surge forward much faster.

As a glacier moves, it reshapes the land beneath it. Rocks frozen into the bottom of the ice act like sandpaper, scraping and polishing the bedrock. Over thousands of years, a glacier can widen a narrow, V-shaped river valley into a broad valley shaped like the letter U. Long scratches left on exposed rock show the direction in which the ice once traveled.

Glaciers also carry material great distances. When the ice finally melts, it drops everything it was carrying. Long ridges of mixed rock and soil, called moraines, mark the places where a glacier's edge once stood. Sometimes a single enormous boulder is left sitting alone in a field, far from any rock of the same type. Such boulders, known as erratics, puzzled early scientists until they realized that ice had carried them there.

Today, glaciers cover about a tenth of Earth's land. Scientists watch them carefully, because changes in their size reveal changes in climate. By studying U-shaped valleys, moraines, and erratics, researchers can also map where glaciers spread during past ice ages, reading the story of ancient ice in landscapes that are now green and warm.

passage:
Look at a map of the eastern United States, and you may notice something curious. A string of cities, among them Trenton, Richmond, and Augusta, lies along an invisible line that runs roughly parallel to the Atlantic coast. These cities were not placed there by accident. They grew up along what geographers call the fall line, and their story shows how geography can shape economic life.

The fall line marks the boundary between two different kinds of land. To the west lie the hard, ancient rocks of the hilly Piedmont region. To the east lies the coastal plain, made of softer layers of sand and clay. Over millions of years, rivers flowing toward the ocean wore away the soft rock of the plain more quickly than the hard rock upstream. As a result, wherever a river crosses from one region to the other, it tumbles over waterfalls and rapids.

For early travelers, these falls were a barrier. Boats could sail upriver from the coast, but they could go no farther once they reached the rapids. Cargo had to be unloaded and carried around the falls or loaded onto wagons heading inland. Places where goods must change from one kind of transport to another often become busy trading centers, because the work of unloading, storing, buying, and selling creates jobs. Warehouses, inns, and markets sprang up at the falls, and small settlements became towns.

The falls offered a second advantage: power. Before electricity, rushing water was one of the most valuable sources of energy available. Water wheels built beside the rapids turned millstones to grind grain into flour and later powered machines that sawed lumber and spun cotton into thread. The same feature that blocked boats could run factories.

Over time, the growth fed on itself. As businesses gathered, workers arrived; as workers arrived, more shops, schools, and roads were built. Even after railroads and highways made river travel less important, many fall line cities kept growing, because they were already established centers of trade and industry.

The fall line reminds us that the locations of cities are rarely random. Physical features such as rivers, harbors, and mountain passes create opportunities, and people tend to settle where those opportunities are greatest.

Look at a map of the eastern United States, and you may notice something curious. A string of cities, among them Trenton, Richmond, and Augusta, lies along an invisible line that runs roughly parallel to the Atlantic coast. These cities were not placed there by accident. They grew up along what geographers call the fall line, and their story shows how geography can shape economic life.

The fall line marks the boundary between two different kinds of land. To the west lie the hard, ancient rocks of the hilly Piedmont region. To the east lies the coastal plain, made of softer layers of sand and clay. Over millions of years, rivers flowing toward the ocean wore away the soft rock of the plain more quickly than the hard rock upstream. As a result, wherever a river crosses from one region to the other, it tumbles over waterfalls and rapids.

For early travelers, these falls were a barrier. Boats could sail upriver from the coast, but they could go no farther once they reached the rapids. Cargo had to be unloaded and carried around the falls or loaded onto wagons heading inland. Places where goods must change from one kind of transport to another often become busy trading centers, because the work of unloading, storing, buying, and selling creates jobs. Warehouses, inns, and markets sprang up at the falls, and small settlements became towns.

The falls offered a second advantage: power. Before electricity, rushing water was one of the most valuable sources of energy available. Water wheels built beside the rapids turned millstones to grind grain into flour and later powered machines that sawed lumber and spun cotton into thread. The same feature that blocked boats could run factories.

Over time, the growth fed on itself. As businesses gathered, workers arrived; as workers arrived, more shops, schools, and roads were built. Even after railroads and highways made river travel less important, many fall line cities kept growing, because they were already established centers of trade and industry.

The fall line reminds us that the locations of cities are rarely random. Physical features such as rivers, harbors, and mountain passes create opportunities, and people tend to settle where those opportunities are greatest.

Leo had lived in Harborview for exactly nine days, and he still could not find his way anywhere without getting hopelessly turned around. His old town had been small enough to cross on a bicycle in fifteen minutes, with streets arranged in a tidy grid. Harborview, by contrast, sprawled along the bay in a tangle of hills and narrow lanes, and every corner seemed to lead somewhere he had not expected.

On the tenth morning, determined to fight back, he packed a sketchbook, a pencil, and a bottle of water and set out to create his own map of the neighborhood.

At first, the work was extremely frustrating, because almost nothing he drew matched what he actually saw. He drew the street outside his apartment far too wide and had to erase it completely. The bakery he thought he had passed twice turned out to be two different bakeries on two different corners. By noon, his paper was smudged and wrinkled, and his map looked less like a town than a plate of spaghetti.

He was sitting on a bench, glaring at the page, when an elderly woman carrying a basket of oranges settled down beside him. She glanced at his sketch with obvious interest. "Ah," she said, "you've discovered the trouble with Harborview. The streets were laid out by goats."

Leo laughed in spite of himself, and the woman introduced herself as Mrs. Okafor and explained that she had lived on Juniper Hill for forty years. Then, pointing to his drawing, she said, "You have Lantern Street running the wrong way; it curves toward the water, not away from it. Everything in this town bends toward the harbor, like flowers turning toward the sun."

That single observation changed everything. Once Leo understood that the streets curved toward the bay, the confusing puzzle gradually began to make sense. He spent the afternoon walking, checking, and redrawing, and by evening he had produced a map that actually worked. He had also included details that no ordinary map would show: the stairway decorated with painted tiles, the bench where Mrs. Okafor rested each morning, and the corner where a gray cat dozed in the window of a secondhand bookstore.

That night, Leo pinned the finished map above his desk. He realized that it was not merely a guide to Harborview's streets but also a record of the first day the unfamiliar town had started to feel like his.

passage:
When a honeybee forager discovers a rich patch of flowers, she faces a communication problem that would challenge any engineer. How can she inform her nestmates, inside a dark hive, where to find food that may be several kilometers away? The answer, decoded by the Austrian biologist Karl von Frisch in the mid-twentieth century, is one of the most remarkable examples of symbolic communication in the animal kingdom.

Von Frisch observed that returning foragers often performed a peculiar routine on the vertical surface of the honeycomb. A bee would run forward in a straight line while vigorously shaking her abdomen, then circle back to her starting point and repeat the run, alternating between left and right loops. He spent years on patient experiments, training marked bees to visit feeding stations at carefully measured locations and then watching them dance. In this way, von Frisch determined that the "waggle dance" encoded two pieces of information. The angle of the straight run, measured relative to vertical, corresponded to the angle between the food source and the sun's position. The duration of the waggle portion indicated distance: the longer the waggle, the farther away the flowers.

The discovery was startling because it implied that bees could translate a direction in the open landscape into an abstract representation on a wall, and that other bees could translate it back. Not everyone was persuaded. In the 1960s, a group of researchers argued that recruits located food primarily by following floral odors carried on the dancer's body, and that the dance itself might convey little useful information. Their experiments showed that scent did play a role, and for a time the debate grew heated.

Resolving the controversy required technology that von Frisch never had. Researchers eventually built small robotic bees that could perform programmed dances in a hive. Some recruits flew toward the locations the robot indicated, even though the robot carried no scent from those sites. Most decisively, a team in the early 2000s attached tiny radar transponders to newly recruited bees and tracked their flights. Recruits that had been moved to an unfamiliar release point flew in the direction, and for roughly the distance, that the dance had specified, demonstrating that they were relying on the dance's information rather than simply searching for familiar smells.

Today, most biologists regard the waggle dance as a genuine symbolic signal, though one supplemented by odor and other cues once recruits approach their target. The episode also offers a lesson about how science proceeds. Von Frisch's interpretation was correct in its essentials, yet the skeptics were not merely obstinate; their challenge exposed the importance of scent and forced researchers to devise more rigorous tests. Von Frisch shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1973. Yet the full confirmation of his insight depended in part on the persistence of those who doubted it.

For centuries, sailors could find their latitude, or position north or south, by measuring the height of the sun or certain stars above the horizon. Longitude, their position east or west, was a far more stubborn problem. Because Earth rotates fifteen degrees every hour, a navigator who knew both the exact time at a home port and the local time aboard ship could calculate longitude from the difference. Local time was comparatively easy to determine by observing the sun at noon. The difficulty lay in preserving the home port's time across thousands of kilometers of ocean.

In principle, a reliable clock would solve the problem. In practice, the finest clocks of the early eighteenth century depended on swinging pendulums, which were useless on a pitching deck. Variations in temperature caused metal components to expand and contract, altering the clock's rate, and humidity thickened the lubricants inside. An error of only a few minutes could place a ship many kilometers from where its crew believed it to be, an uncertainty that contributed to costly shipwrecks.

In 1714, the British government offered a substantial prize for a practical method of determining longitude at sea. Many prominent scientists assumed the solution would emerge from astronomy, perhaps by using the predictable movement of the moon against the background stars as a kind of celestial clock. John Harrison, a largely self-taught carpenter and clockmaker from the north of England, pursued a mechanical answer instead.

Harrison devoted more than four decades to the challenge. His first three timekeepers were large, intricate machines. They included ingenious innovations, such as linked metal bars that compensated for temperature changes and bearings that reduced the need for oil. Yet each fell short of his own exacting standards. His breakthrough came with a fourth design that abandoned the bulky approach altogether: a timepiece only somewhat larger than a pocket watch. On a voyage to the Caribbean in the early 1760s, it reportedly lost only a few seconds over many weeks at sea.

Even this triumph did not bring immediate reward. The officials responsible for the prize, some of whom favored the astronomical method, questioned whether Harrison's results could be replicated, demanded additional trials, and insisted that he fully disclose his design. Only after years of negotiation, and when he was in his eighties, did Harrison receive payments approaching the full amount.

Harrison's persistence nonetheless transformed navigation. Within several decades, copies of his design, known as marine chronometers, were becoming standard equipment on long voyages, and navigators often used astronomical and mechanical methods together to verify each other. The story suggests that a problem regarded as the province of theorists may sometimes yield to the patient work of a skilled craftsman.

Beneath the floor of nearly every forest lies a vast, hidden partnership. The roots of most plants are entwined with the threads of fungi. Together they form associations called mycorrhizae, from the Greek words for "fungus" and "root." The fungal threads, called hyphae, are far thinner than even the finest roots. This allows them to penetrate tiny pores in the soil and absorb water and mineral nutrients, such as phosphorus, that roots alone would struggle to reach. In exchange, the plant supplies the fungus with sugars produced through photosynthesis. Neither partner is merely a passenger; each provides something the other cannot easily obtain on its own.

This exchange is ancient. Fossil evidence suggests that fungi were associated with some of the earliest land plants more than four hundred million years ago. Many botanists believe that such partnerships helped plants colonize barren continents in the first place. Today, the great majority of plant species form such relationships. Experiments show that many grow poorly when their fungal partners are removed.

In recent decades, researchers have investigated a more surprising possibility. Because a single fungus can connect to the roots of several plants, and a single plant can host several fungi, forests may be laced with underground networks linking trees of different ages and even different species. Using chemical tracers, some studies have detected the movement of carbon from one tree to another through these connections. Such findings inspired the popular nickname "the wood wide web" and the appealing notion that mature "mother trees" deliberately nourish their seedlings.

Other scientists urge caution. They note that many of the field studies were small. It is also difficult to rule out alternative routes by which carbon could travel through soil, and the amounts transferred were sometimes too small to matter much to a tree's survival. Moreover, describing trees as devoted parents may project human motives onto organisms whose interactions could be explained by simpler processes, such as fungi distributing resources according to their own needs. A recent review of the evidence concluded that, while mycorrhizal networks clearly exist, several widely repeated claims about their role in forest communication and sharing rest on limited data.

This debate does not diminish the importance of mycorrhizae. The basic exchange of nutrients for sugars is firmly established and essential to most ecosystems on land. Instead, it illustrates a recurring tension in science between a compelling story and the slower work of verification. The underground world remains difficult to observe directly, and the most accurate description of forest networks may ultimately prove less romantic, but no less fascinating, than the popular version.

passage:
Many of the most celebrated wall paintings of the Italian Renaissance were created using a demanding technique known as buon fresco, or "true fresco." Unlike an artist working on canvas, who can revise a composition over weeks or months, the fresco painter worked against a chemical deadline, and the discipline this imposed shaped both the methods and the appearance of the art.

The process began with the preparation of the wall. Workers applied several layers of plaster made from lime, sand, and water, each finer than the last. The final layer, called the intonaco, was spread only over an area that the painter expected to complete in a single session. While this layer was still damp, the artist brushed on pigments mixed with nothing but water. As the plaster dried, a chemical reaction with carbon dioxide in the air transformed the lime into a hard, crystalline form of calcium carbonate. This reaction locked the particles of pigment into the surface of the wall itself. The color did not merely rest on top of the plaster; it became part of it.

This chemistry gave true fresco its remarkable durability, but it also left little room for error. Once the plaster had set, typically within a day, the paint could no longer bond with it. A serious mistake required chiseling away the section and starting over with fresh plaster. Consequently, painters divided large compositions into sections called giornate, an Italian word derived from "day," and carefully planned the sequence in which they would be painted. The seams between these daily patches often followed the outlines of figures or architectural details, where they would be least noticeable. Modern conservators, examining frescoes under angled light, can still trace these joins and thereby reconstruct the order, and sometimes the pace, of an artist's work.

Not every pigment could survive the chemically harsh environment of wet lime, so fresco painters relied on a limited palette composed largely of earth-based colors. Certain brilliant blues and other sensitive pigments had to be applied afterward on dry plaster, a method called fresco secco. These additions, attached with glue or egg rather than bound chemically into the wall, were far less permanent; in many surviving works they have flaked away, leaving areas that appear strangely faded compared with the robust colors surrounding them.

The constraints of fresco thus left their mark on the finished paintings. The necessity of working quickly encouraged confident, economical brushwork and meticulous advance planning, often with full-scale drawings transferred to the wall before painting began. Far from merely limiting artists, the technique's demands helped produce works whose colors have endured for five centuries.

At five o'clock in the morning, the marsh was the color of weak tea, and Ruth was convinced that volunteering for the spring bird survey had been the most serious miscalculation of her sixteen years. Her cousin Dev, who had persuaded her to come, was already crouched at the edge of the boardwalk with a notebook balanced on his knee, his binoculars raised toward a stand of reeds that, as far as Ruth could determine, contained nothing whatsoever.

"Listen," he whispered.

Ruth listened obediently, cataloguing each sound in turn: the steady hum of insects, the distant grumble of a delivery truck on the highway, and the unpleasant squelch of her own sneakers, which had proven considerably less waterproof than their packaging had advertised. Nothing she heard resembled a bird.

Dev made a small mark in his notebook and murmured, "Marsh wren, two of them, actually, answering each other from opposite ends of the reeds."

She was prepared to accuse him of inventing it, but then, as though the reeds had decided to settle the argument, a rattling, bubbling song spilled out of them, followed almost instantly by a reply from farther away. Ruth realized, with mild irritation, that she had been hearing the sound for several minutes and had simply filed it away with the insects.

For the next two hours, Dev taught her to separate the morning into its individual threads. The liquid three-note phrase belonged to a red-winged blackbird; the dry, insistent chip came from a sparrow that refused to reveal itself; the thin whistle overhead was a hawk circling patiently above the water. Gradually, the marsh, which had seemed empty and monotonous, became crowded and argumentative, as though she had wandered into a room where everyone had been conversing all along and she was only now beginning to understand the language.

What surprised her most was not the number of birds but the transformation in her own attention. Ordinarily, Ruth moved through the world at the speed of her phone, glancing, evaluating, and moving on without a second thought. Here, a single unremarkable patch of cattails rewarded ten minutes of stillness with a flicker of movement, a flash of yellow, a bird that would have remained invisible to anyone in a hurry.

When the survey concluded, Dev tallied the results: forty-one species. Ruth had personally identified six, and she privately suspected that at least two of those had been fortunate guesses rather than genuine recognitions. Nevertheless, as they walked back toward the parking lot, she caught herself pausing at a song from the hedgerow, head tilted, attempting to name it before Dev could.

"Same time next week?" he asked, not entirely concealing his grin.

Ruth pretended to deliberate, frowning theatrically at the condition of her sneakers. "Maybe," she said, which they both understood perfectly well to mean yes.

At five o'clock in the morning, the marsh was the color of weak tea, and Ruth was convinced that volunteering for the spring bird survey had been the most serious miscalculation of her sixteen years. Her cousin Dev, who had persuaded her to come, was already crouched at the edge of the boardwalk with a notebook balanced on his knee, his binoculars raised toward a stand of reeds that, as far as Ruth could determine, contained nothing whatsoever.

"Listen," he whispered.

Ruth listened obediently, cataloguing each sound in turn: the steady hum of insects, the distant grumble of a delivery truck on the highway, and the unpleasant squelch of her own sneakers, which had proven considerably less waterproof than their packaging had advertised. Nothing she heard resembled a bird.

Dev made a small mark in his notebook and murmured, "Marsh wren, two of them, actually, answering each other from opposite ends of the reeds."

She was prepared to accuse him of inventing it, but then, as though the reeds had decided to settle the argument, a rattling, bubbling song spilled out of them, followed almost instantly by a reply from farther away. Ruth realized, with mild irritation, that she had been hearing the sound for several minutes and had simply filed it away with the insects.

For the next two hours, Dev taught her to separate the morning into its individual threads. The liquid three-note phrase belonged to a red-winged blackbird; the dry, insistent chip came from a sparrow that refused to reveal itself; the thin whistle overhead was a hawk circling patiently above the water. Gradually, the marsh, which had seemed empty and monotonous, became crowded and argumentative, as though she had wandered into a room where everyone had been conversing all along and she was only now beginning to understand the language.

What surprised her most was not the number of birds but the transformation in her own attention. Ordinarily, Ruth moved through the world at the speed of her phone, glancing, evaluating, and moving on without a second thought. Here, a single unremarkable patch of cattails rewarded ten minutes of stillness with a flicker of movement, a flash of yellow, a bird that would have remained invisible to anyone in a hurry.

When the survey concluded, Dev tallied the results: forty-one species. Ruth had personally identified six, and she privately suspected that at least two of those had been fortunate guesses rather than genuine recognitions. Nevertheless, as they walked back toward the parking lot, she caught herself pausing at a song from the hedgerow, head tilted, attempting to name it before Dev could.

"Same time next week?" he asked, not entirely concealing his grin.

Ruth pretended to deliberate, frowning theatrically at the condition of her sneakers. "Maybe," she said, which they both understood perfectly well to mean yes.
